motif: Our running example is the sentence from the paper's own attention plots: "The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just", drawn as a row of rounded word tiles left to right. Grey tiles are plain words, the tile for "its" is highlighted amber as the query, and violet curved arcs show attention links, with thicker arcs for stronger weights. Slow orange arrows mark sequential RNN steps, green marks parallel computation, and red marks costs or limits.

scenes.title: RNNs must read one word at a time
scenes.narration: To understand "its", a recurrent network walks the sentence word by word, each step waiting on the last. That chain can't be split across the GPU, so training long sentences is slow.
scenes.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

diagram.title: RNNs must read one word at a time
diagram.caption: A recurrent network computes each hidden state from the previous one plus the current word, so this 13-token sentence takes 13 steps in strict order (p. 2). Table 1 lists O(n) sequential operations for recurrent layers (p. 6).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the time step slider, then press “Try computing all words at once” to see which steps are blocked.
diagram.html: RNNs must read one word at a time

explorables.label: Hidden state hₜ
explorables.blurb: Each circle is the RNN's memory after reading one more word. It is computed from the previous circle plus the current word, so it cannot exist before its predecessor.
explorables.quote: Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states ht, as a function of the previous hidden state ht−1 and the input for position t.

explorables.label: The sequential chain
explorables.blurb: The orange arrows are dependencies: step t must finish before step t+1 can begin. Within a single sentence the work cannot be split across GPU cores, and longer sentences make this worse.
explorables.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

explorables.label: O(n) sequential steps
explorables.blurb: For n words a recurrent layer needs n steps run one after another. The paper's Table 1 contrasts this with O(1) for self-attention.
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

explorables.label: Law → its path length
explorables.blurb: To link “its” back to “Law”, information has to pass through every hidden state in between. The paper argues that longer paths like this make long-range dependencies harder to learn.
explorables.quote: One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network.

explorables.label: Why “its”?
explorables.blurb: “its” refers back to “Law”, which is a classic anaphora. The paper's own attention plots show heads that link these two words directly.
explorables.quote: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution.

scenes.title: Convolutions parallelize but distant words stay far apart
scenes.narration: Convolutional models like ByteNet and ConvS2S process all words at once. But linking "its" back to "Law" still takes several stacked layers, and the gap grows with distance, which makes long-range links harder to learn.
scenes.quote: In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet.

diagram.title: Convolutions parallelize but distant words stay far apart
diagram.caption: Convolutional models such as ByteNet and ConvS2S compute every position in parallel. Relating two positions still takes more operations as they get farther apart: linearly for ConvS2S, logarithmically for ByteNet (p. 2; Table 1, p. 6; p. 7).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the target-word slider away from “its”, then switch between contiguous and dilated kernels and watch the red path and layer count change.
diagram.html:

Illustrative toy setup: kernel width 3, with dilation doubling each layer (1, 2, 4, 8). Green marks positions computed in parallel, red marks the path cost, and the dashed violet arc marks a direct attention link. Click any word tile to make it the target.

explorables.label: Why stack layers?
explorables.blurb: A kernel only covers a small window of neighbouring words. To connect two distant words, the signal has to pass up through several layers stacked on top of each other.
explorables.quote: A single convolutional layer with kernel width k < n does not connect all pairs of input and output positions.

explorables.label: Contiguous vs dilated
explorables.blurb: The shaded cone is what the top node for “its” can see. Contiguous kernels widen it by a fixed amount per layer, so reach grows linearly (O(n/k) layers). Dilated kernels skip positions, so reach grows exponentially and you need only O(log_k(n)) layers.
explorables.quote: Doing so requires a stack of O(n/k) convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or O(logk(n)) in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network.

explorables.label: Path length
explorables.blurb: The red path is the route a signal takes between the two words. The paper argues that longer paths make long-range dependencies harder to learn.
explorables.quote: The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies

explorables.label: Table 1 path lengths
explorables.blurb: Table 1 compares layer types by the maximum path length between two positions. Recurrent layers need O(n), convolutions need O(log_k(n)) with dilation, and self-attention needs O(1).
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

scenes.title: Let every word look directly at every other word
scenes.narration: The Transformer drops recurrence and convolution entirely. With self-attention, "its" connects to "Law" in a single step. Every pair of words is one hop apart, and all the arcs are computed in parallel.
scenes.quote: In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.

diagram.title: Let every word look directly at every other word
diagram.caption: The Transformer relies entirely on attention instead of recurrence or convolution (p. 2). A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations, while a recurrent layer needs O(n) (p. 6).
diagram.tryHint: Try: click “application” or “The” to make it the query, then hover a far-away word to see that it is still one hop.
diagram.html:
Path length: 1 hop · O(1)Sequential ops: O(1) · all links at onceCost: 13 × 13 = 169 pair scores · O(n²·d)
Click a word to make it the query · arc thickness = illustrative weights

explorables.label: Self-attention
explorables.blurb: Each violet arc is a direct link from the query word to another word in the same sentence. The layer builds each word's new representation by mixing in information from all the others according to these link strengths.
explorables.quote: Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence.

explorables.label: One-hop path length
explorables.blurb: Any two words are joined by a single attention step, however far apart they are. A recurrent layer needs a chain of O(n) steps, and shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

explorables.label: Computed in parallel
explorables.blurb: No link has to wait for an earlier one, so all words are processed at once instead of one step at a time. This is why the base model reached state-of-the-art translation after about 12 hours on 8 GPUs.
explorables.quote: The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

explorables.label: The n² cost
explorables.blurb: Linking every pair means n × n scores, giving O(n²·d) work per layer. This is cheaper than recurrence when the sentence length n is below the model dimension d. For very long inputs, the authors suggest restricting attention to a local neighborhood.
explorables.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

scenes.title: Attention is a soft lookup: query, keys, values
scenes.narration: "its" sends out a query and every word offers a key and a value. The model takes query-key dot products, divides them by the square root of the key size, and applies a softmax. The resulting weights blend the values.
scenes.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

diagram.title: Attention is a soft lookup: query, keys, values
diagram.caption: Scaled dot-product attention compares the query “its” with every key, divides each dot product by √dk, and applies a softmax. The resulting weights average the values (pp. 3–4). Each head uses dk = 64, and without the scaling, large dot products saturate the softmax (p. 4).
diagram.tryHint: Try: untick “Scale by 1/√dk” and drag the key size up to 512 to watch the softmax collapse onto one word.
diagram.html: Scores are illustrative (unit-scale q·k per word). Unscaled q·k is modeled as growing like √dk because its variance is dk (p. 4). The paper uses dk = 64 per head.

explorables.label: The query
explorables.blurb: The word doing the looking, here “its”, is turned into a query vector. That vector is compared against every word's key to decide where to look.
explorables.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

explorables.label: Keys and dot products
explorables.blurb: Each word offers a key, and a query–key dot product measures how well the two match. All the dot products for a sentence come out of a single matrix multiplication, which is why this method is fast.
explorables.quote: dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

explorables.label: Dividing by √dk
explorables.blurb: When the components have unit variance, a dot product over dk dimensions has variance dk, so raw scores grow with the key size. Dividing by √dk keeps the scores in a range where the softmax still has useful gradients.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: Softmax weights
explorables.blurb: The softmax turns the scaled scores into positive weights that sum to 1. The lookup is soft: every word gets some share, and the best matches get most of it.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Weighted sum of values
explorables.blurb: The output for “its” is a weighted average of all the value vectors. In this illustration, most of the mix comes from “Law” and “application”.
explorables.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

scenes.title: Sine waves stamp word order onto the tiles
scenes.narration: Attention alone ignores word order, so each tile gets a sinusoidal position signal added to its embedding. These tiles flow through six encoder layers and six decoder layers, and masking stops the decoder from peeking at future words.
scenes.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

diagram.title: Sine waves stamp word order onto the tiles
diagram.caption: The Transformer has no recurrence or convolution, so a sinusoidal position signal is added to each word embedding (p. 6). The tiles then pass through 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, and masking keeps the decoder from seeing later words (p. 3, 5).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the position slider and watch each sine wave give that position its own pattern of values.
diagram.html: pos 8 → “its”

explorables.label: Sine waves per dimension
explorables.blurb: Each dimension of the position signal is a sine or cosine wave, and each pair of dimensions uses a slower frequency than the one before. Taken together, the values at a given position form a pattern that no other position shares.
explorables.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π.

explorables.label: Added, not appended
explorables.blurb: The position signal has the same size as the word embedding (512 in the paper), so the two are added together. Each tile then carries both what the word is and where it sits.
explorables.quote: To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension dmodel as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed.

explorables.label: Relative positions
explorables.blurb: The authors picked sinusoids because the signal at a shifted position is a linear function of the signal at the original position. They expected this to make relative offsets easy to learn. Learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results.
explorables.quote: We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos+k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.

explorables.label: 6 + 6 layers
explorables.blurb: The encoder stacks six identical layers, each with self-attention followed by a feed-forward network. The decoder also has six layers and adds a third sub-layer that attends to the encoder's output.
explorables.quote: The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, positionwise fully connected feed-forward network.

explorables.label: Decoder mask
explorables.blurb: In decoder self-attention, links to later positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, which is shown as red cells here. As a result, each prediction can only use the words already produced.
explorables.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

scenes.title: Better translations at a fraction of the cost
scenes.narration: The big model scores 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German and 41.8 on English-to-French after 3.5 days on eight GPUs. The base model trains in 12 hours and still beats earlier ensembles. It also reaches 92.7 F1 on parsing.
scenes.quote: On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the big transformer model (Transformer (big) in Table 2) outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4.

diagram.title: Better translations at a fraction of the cost
diagram.caption: Table 2 (p. 8): both Transformer sizes match or beat earlier models on WMT 2014 translation while using far fewer training FLOPs. The base model beats every earlier En→De result and trails on En→Fr. Table 4 (p. 10) shows the model also transfers to English constituency parsing.
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the training-budget slider left and watch which models remain affordable, then switch to EN→FR.
diagram.html: The catch: every word attends to every word, so each self-attention layer costs O(n²·d) (Table 1, p. 6).

explorables.label: Training cost (FLOPs)
explorables.blurb: Cost is an estimate, not a measurement. It multiplies training time, the number of GPUs, and each GPU's sustained single-precision throughput, which is 9.5 TFLOPS for a P100.
explorables.quote: We estimate the number of floating point operations used to train a model by multiplying the training time, the number of GPUs used, and an estimate of the sustained single-precision floating-point capacity of each GPU

explorables.label: BLEU on newstest2014
explorables.blurb: BLEU scores translation quality by overlap with reference translations, so higher is better. All translation numbers in the chart come from the WMT 2014 newstest2014 test sets.
explorables.quote: The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.

explorables.label: Parsing F1 (WSJ 23)
explorables.blurb: A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning reaches 91.3 F1 trained on WSJ alone and 92.7 F1 semi-supervised. Among the models listed, only the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (93.3) and one multi-task model (93.0) score higher.
explorables.quote: Our results in Table 4 show that despite the lack of task-specific tuning our model performs surprisingly well, yielding better results than all previously reported models with the exception of the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar

scenes.title: Every-word-to-every-word gets costly for long inputs
scenes.narration: All those arcs scale with the square of sentence length, which hurts on very long inputs like images or audio. Output generation is also still one word at a time. The authors leave restricted, local attention for future work.
scenes.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

diagram.title: Every-word-to-every-word gets costly for long inputs
diagram.caption: A self-attention layer costs O(n²·d), while attention restricted to a neighborhood of size r would cost O(r·n·d) but stretch the maximum path length to O(n/r) (pp. 6–7). The authors leave local attention, and less sequential generation, for future work (p. 10).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the sequence length to the right, then switch restricted attention on and off and watch which arcs from “its” are lost.
diagram.html:
Every-word-to-every-word gets costly for long inputs
Trade-off: max path length O(1) → O(n/r)
Arc weights and sequence lengths are illustrative. Costs O(n²·d) and O(r·n·d) are from Table 1 (p. 6). Restricted attention is proposed, not tested, in the paper.

explorables.label: Quadratic cost
explorables.blurb: Every word scores every other word, so one self-attention layer costs O(n²·d) (Table 1). That is cheap for sentences, where n is usually smaller than d, but it grows fast for long inputs.
explorables.quote: self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d, which is most often the case with sentence representations

explorables.label: Restricted window r
explorables.blurb: The authors suggest a fix in which each position attends only to a neighborhood of r words around it, cutting the cost to O(r·n·d). They propose it but do not test it in the paper.
explorables.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

explorables.label: Longer paths trade-off
explorables.blurb: A window costs reach. Distant words, like 'Law' for 'its' in this example, can no longer connect in one step, so the maximum path length grows from O(1) to O(n/r).
explorables.quote: centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r). We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.

explorables.label: One word at a time
explorables.blurb: Training runs in parallel, but the decoder is auto-regressive. It emits one symbol, feeds it back in, then emits the next. The authors name less sequential generation as a research goal.
explorables.quote: Given z, the decoder then generates an output sequence (y1, ..., ym) of symbols one element at a time.

explorables.label: Images, audio, video
explorables.blurb: Non-text inputs such as images, audio and video give much longer sequences than sentences, which is where the n² cost bites. The authors plan to extend the Transformer to them with local, restricted attention.
explorables.quote: We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video.

questions.title: Why can attention link distant words in a single step?
questions.hook: An RNN passes a signal through n steps to connect the first and last word, while self-attention connects every pair at once, trading sequential depth for n² work.
questions.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

questions.title: How does a query pick which values to read?
questions.hook: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: every key gets a score against the query, and the output blends all values by those scores rather than fetching just one.
questions.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

questions.title: Why divide the dot products by √dₖ?
questions.hook: Without the scale factor, dot-product variance grows with dₖ, so softmax saturates to near one-hot and its gradients almost vanish.
questions.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

questions.title: Why use 8 small heads instead of one big one?
questions.hook: One head has to average everything into a single blend, while eight 64-dim heads at the same total cost can each track a different relation, such as syntax or anaphora.
questions.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

questions.title: How does masking stop the decoder from cheating?
questions.hook: A triangle of −∞ entries in the score matrix, together with shifting the outputs right by one, lets the model train on all positions in parallel without ever seeing the future.
questions.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

questions.title: How do sine waves tell the model word order?
questions.hook: Attention by itself ignores word order, so each position gets a fingerprint of sinusoids at geometrically spaced frequencies; any fixed offset is then a linear function of that fingerprint.
questions.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid.
